utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Meek and Mr. Bourgon. That's about it. For the prosecution, I see Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, and Mr. Mitchell. All right. I understand there is some preliminary. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. Just a brief preliminary with respect to the next witness, and if we may move into private session just for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring the witness in. Incidentally, we are going to give our ruling on yesterday's Gvero Defence team submission for certification. So we are seized with an oral Gvero Defence team submission for certification to appeal the oral decision on the Prosecution motion -- Trial Chamber's oral decision on the Prosecution motion of 1st of February, 2008, to wit to add Ms. Emma Sayer to the 65 ter list and Prosecution reply. We will not address the submissions related to the alleged errors in the Trial Chamber's decision, which of course is not relevant to the test under the Rules. With respect to the first prong of the test, the Gvero Defence team emphasizes the import of the issue as acknowledged by the Trial Chamber, which makes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm somewhat unhappy the witness hearing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sayer, if you could leave the courtroom for a while, please. I think you're right, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With reference to the first prong of the test, the Gvero Defence team emphasizes the importance of the issue, as acknowledged by the Trial Chamber, namely, that -- which makes the issue one which would significantly affect the outcome of the trial. The Trial Chamber notes that while the proposed evidence of Ms. Sayer goes indeed to an important issue in terms of the trial, that does not automatically mean that the issue for certification is one which would significantly affect the outcome of the trial. The Trial Chamber, in fact, is of the opinion that given the limited scope of this issue and the manner in which the Trial Chamber has proposed to address any fair trial concerns in its decision, the first aspect of the test has not been met. While not strictly necessary, we are also dealing with the second prong, with regard to which we note that the standard to be met under Rule 73(b), the Gvero Defence team submits that an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber will affect the Defence case and that it would clarify the case to be made by the Defence, and in particular if it is necessary to recall the witnesses who have testified already for the Prosecution. However, the Trial Chamber finds that the Gvero Defence team has not shown how this may materially advance the proceedings. We therefore hold that the standard in Rule 73(b) has not been met and deny certification. So I apologise to you, Mr. Josse. Actually, while I was reading, I was thinking precisely on whether she should be here or not, but, anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- thanks for raising the matter. So let's bring her in again, please. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I was just standing for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sayer, good afternoon to you. Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're about to start giving evidence. Incidentally, you are also the last witness in the Prosecution case in chief, in this case. Our intention is to finish with your testimony today so that you can return back to your work. Now before you start your testimony, madam, you are required, under our rules, to give us a solemn undertaking -- make a solemn undertaking that you will be testifying the truth. That's the equivalent of an oath in your jurisdiction. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of our solemn declaration. Go ahead, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, ma'am. Mr. Thayer will go first, and then you will be cross-examined by some or all of the Defence teams. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My full name is Emma Lucinda Sayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I am 37 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you tell us just a little about your educational background, briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I have a degree, a first degree, from Nottingham University in Russian and Serbo-Croat after following the normal U.K. education system until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And allow me just briefly to summarise your military service history, and correct me at any point if I've misstated anything. Your service in the British Army began with a year at Sandhurst, after which you volunteered for a six-month tour of duty in Vitez and Gornji Vakuf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that was in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between question and answers for the sake of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please comply. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Subsequent to that tour, you returned to the U.K. and debriefed refugees and returning soldiers and liaison officers from the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this time, you received additional language training?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: After that, you were posted in the U.K. to run an army domestic security unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then in June of 1995, you began serving as a liaison officer and interpreter, working for General Rupert Smith at UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina Command in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You served there until 1996, after which you were deployed to Saudi Arabia in connection with monitoring the no-fly zone over Southern Iraq?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 1997, you were deployed in Northern Ireland as adjutant with the Force Intelligence Unit?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In 1998, you were deployed in New York, where you worked at the UN Special Commission on Iraq as a member of a identification team or a site identification team regarding weapons of mass destruction?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in 1999, you returned to Northern Ireland, and then served in Kosovo as a media officer?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you left the army in 2000 at the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Turning your attention now to your service with General Smith in Sarajevo, can you briefly describe what were your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My primary role was the liaison officer and interpreter for the Armija BiH and Bosnia civilian politicians within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And who worked with the Serb civilian and BSA side in your role?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Captain Tom Dibb held that role.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you, on occasion, attend meetings with the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I only very occasionally was required to attend meetings with the Serb side when Captain Dibb was deployed on alternate duty or was on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to get right to July of 1995, ma'am. At that time, what surname were you using?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My surname at that time was "Bliss."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall accompanying General Smith to Zepa at some time in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the exact dates on which you travelled to Zepa? With General Smith?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were those dates, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The 25th, 26th, and 27th of July were the primary dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to briefly show you a couple of reports from that period of time, not to discuss them in substance, but just to tie in these dates that you've just recited for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see P02747, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the summary portion, it indicates that this is a report of a meeting between General Smith and Generals Mladic and Gvero at the Jela Restaurant on the 25th of July. Were you present for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I was present for this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was this the first time you recall meeting General Gvero in person?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I believe it was the first time I had met General Gvero, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could just scroll down a little bit and give you an opportunity briefly to -- if we could scroll all the way down, just to reacquaint yourself. And if we could go to page 2, please, and this is of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The report indicates that Zepa dominated the two-hour meeting and that the meeting was then resumed in Zepa. With respect to the meeting at the restaurant, was there anything that stood out or still stands out in your mind about that meeting that can place it for you and place yourself there?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I particularly recall the conversation about Bihac, which is annotated in paragraph 6 on, I believe, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think the Serbo-Croat version, we need to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you accompany General Smith when this meeting reconvened at the check-point in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could see 6D00108, please. And we'll just wait until the B/C/S is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 26th of July regarding the situation in Zepa. Have you seen this report, ma'am, recently?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And although it is dated the 26th, having reviewed it, what date -- what is the date of the events which this report memorialises?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The events summarised in this report occurred on the 25th of July, so the day preceding the date at the top of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could just scroll or flip to the next page, please. There we have the heading of the report of the various meetings between General Smith and Mladic in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is there anything about the events of this day that particularly sticks out in your mind, as you've had a chance to review these reports again?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I particularly remember reconvening in Zepa and also the meeting between General Smith and Mr. Torlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there anything in particular about that meeting that sticks out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment, madam. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. An objection. This doesn't fall within the ambit of the evidence that this witness has been asked to come here and testify about. It falls outside of 65 ter, in short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I said, I'm really trying to nail down these dates through specific recollections that the witness has of specific events that stick out in her mind from these meetings. That's why I'm -- I'm not going in any great detail, I'm just asking her, "Is there anything particular about this meeting that sticks out in your mind today?" This was put in a proofing note which was distributed to my friends. It's not in the 65 ter summary. Some of these details came out in proofing. And in fact, actually, it's in the witness statement, I'm sorry, not the proofing note, so it's actually been disclosed much earlier. But, again, it's simply to try to tie down her recollection to these specific days and events, because I imagine that the dates and the sequence are going to be a matter of some discussion. And I'm trying to move through it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Having heard you, Mr. Thayer, although we do understand the point raised by Mr. Josse, I think we can safely proceed, provided you restrict yourself -- you limit yourself to what you said and the witness also keeps that in mind. So do you wish to repeat the question, Mr. Thayer, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll just follow up on it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you mentioned a conversation between General Smith and Mr. Torlak. What is it about the conversation that sticks out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Specifically, during that conversation General Smith asked Mr. Torlak whether there was anybody that wished to remain within the enclave of Zepa, and I distinctly recall the look of shock or disbelief on Mr. Torlak's face, and he replied that, no, nobody was wanting to stay in the enclave because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can just flip to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we see here this summarises the meeting that General Smith had with Mr. Torlak. What role did you play, if any, in creating or writing this report?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I authored the majority of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just flip to the very last page, please. Next page, and all the way at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do we see a signature there that you recognise at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there was a reference at paragraph 11 in this report to returning to Zepa the next day, a discussion about a plan to return on the 26th. Do you recall whether or not General Smith returned to Zepa, in fact, the next day, the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that we returned on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Moving along, if we may see P02946. This is a report describing the situation in Zepa, summary, as at 0800 hours, 28 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, having reviewed this report recently, ma'am, what is the date of the events that are summarised in this report?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The date of the events summarised in this report is the 27th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you present for the events that are described in this report happening in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I was present with General Smith in Zepa when we met with the three members of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, is there anything that stands out in your mind which ties this date of the 27th to your recollection of being there?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically annotated in paragraph 4 was the use of the word "liquidate" by General Mladic when discussing what would happen to the men left in Zepa who refused to surrender their weapons after the deadline that he had set of 1800.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to the best of your recollection, ma'am, was this day, the 27th of July, the last day on which you accompanied General Smith to Zepa or did you go down on another day at some point after that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's an appallingly leading question on an essential part of this witness's evidence, the use of the words "last day."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. Could you rephrase your question, Mr. Thayer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked her whether this was the last day or whether there was another day after that, whether or not she went down. I can simply ask, "Do you recall what day was your last day in Zepa," if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be better, not that it makes much difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My final day in Zepa with General Smith was the 27th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, ma'am. Where was Tom Dibb, to your knowledge, during these days when you were in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Actually, the only reason I was in Zepa was because Tom Dibb had been reassigned to work with Colonel Coiffet, who was deputy chief of staff of the UNPROFOR headquarters, and he was actually in Zepa and involved with Colonel Coiffet throughout that period within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to ask you about an encounter you had at a check-point. I don't think it's any surprise what I'm asking you about. So can you just tell us about -- about this encounter you had at this check-point? Just take it -- take it from the top. Please tell the Court as much as you can remember about what happened.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: On the final day in Zepa, so the 27th, we had had this meeting with the Zepa War Presidency, and we had agreed that we would take the message that they had signed the agreement back to Sarajevo and report what had happened that day to Minister Muratovic and President Izetbegovic, so my recollection is we left quite late, you know, sort of -- I can't say exactly what time, but sort of very -- sort of early evening would be my recollection. And as we were -- as we left the enclave on our way back to Sarajevo, we went past a number of different check-points, and at one of them we met General Gvero. And our vehicle stopped, and there was a very short exchange between ourselves and General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe just the number of people that you recall being in General Smith's party on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: We were travelling in two vehicles, and my recollection is that there were between seven and eight of us on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not Colonel Baxter was among these individuals?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't recall that General Baxter was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall whether there were any members of General Smith's security team with you at this time?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I recall there being at least three members of his security team there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of them?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what is the name of the one person you recall?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The person that I recall being there was Ginge Davidson.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is there any reason, in your mind, why you don't recall the names of anybody else on the security detail?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Because of the nature of our visits to Zepa, the normal bodyguard team had been supplemented, and it wasn't always the same team that accompanied us. So Ginge Davidson was the senior member of that team, so he was always there, and the other members of the team varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would General Smith typically travel with any communications officers, in general?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that was his practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And without referring to any nationality or particular unit, do you recall there being any communications officers at this encounter? And if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I believe there were two communications officers present on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, without referring to any nationality or unit, were there any other personnel that you recall travelling with General Smith on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you take us step by step, as best as you can remember, what happened when you actually arrived at this check-point?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: It was our practice that the interpreter/liaison officer would sit in the front of the vehicle, and their role was to get out of the vehicle and negotiate any issues that we encountered getting through check-points. So my recollection is as we approached this check-point, there was a rather smart-looking dark car, and we came to a halt. And I got out of the vehicle and had a short exchange with General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you recall, to the best of your ability, what that exchange involved? What did he say to you, what did you say to him, please, as best as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, he asked me whether we were finished, whether that was us done in Zepa and was there anybody left. I recall taking that to mean whether any UNPROFOR headquarters personnel left in the enclave. And I recall saying that we were on our way back to Sarajevo and that Colonel Coiffet and Captain Dibb remained in the enclave. And -- and there was an exchange where I had the impression that he was going into the enclave and would then expect to see Colonel Coiffet and Captain Dibb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on this conversation that you had with General Gvero, did you gain any impression of what his purpose was in heading into Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My impression was that he was going to see what was left, you know, what was going on, what the situation was at that time in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall General Smith being present or a party in any sense to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My recollection was that as was normal at check-points, it was very rare for General Smith to actually leave the vehicle because of the security risk, so my recollection is that I was relaying these exchanges through an open door in the back of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple more questions, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see P02947. This is a report of a meeting held in Mrkonjic Grad on the 31st of July at the Balkana Motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you present for this meeting, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm I was present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall General Gvero being present for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I clearly recall General Gvero being present for this meeting, as he actually met us initially, because General Mladic was very late joining us, and we had a long conversation that I interpreted about ploughing and scything with a plough, because -- and the reason I recall is because I didn't know the Serbian name for a scythe, and General Gvero got one of the motel employees to actually go and fetch one so that he could explain that the area was very noted for its competitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall when the last time was when you saw General Gvero in person?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: This was -- the 31st of July was my final encounter with General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this conversation at the check-point with General Gvero, or at any time thereafter, do you recall General Gvero saying that he was in command or in charge of the Zepa operation? Do you remember him ever saying anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, I don't recall him using the term "I'm in command in Zepa," or I don't recall it coming up in conversation on the 31st of July in Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Or how about during the encounter or at any time from the encounter at the check-point on; do you recall ever hearing that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No. My recollection, from our exchange at the check-point on the 27th, was that he was going into the enclave, but I don't recall him saying he was going to take command. I recall -- you know, the impression I had was that he was going to ascertain the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The last couple of questions I have are with respect to a video clip which you've seen in the last couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see P02491, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the video seems to start at one hour two minutes and 40.6 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and we can roll any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the video stopped at one hour two minutes and 50.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in this still?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you could describe, moving from right to left on the frame.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The people in uniform, moving from the right of the frame to the left as I'm looking at it, General Gvero, General Smith and General Mladic, and you can just see me in between -- sort of right behind General Mladic and General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's keep rolling, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've stopped at one hour two minutes 58.1 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this frame? And if you do, if you would describe who they are, moving from left to right on the frame.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And moving from left to right, the man standing, taking his jacket off, is Colonel Baxter. Just in front of him, the man taking his seat is General Rupert Smith. And that's the view of the back of my head, already seated, at the front of the frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we've paused it at one hour three minutes and 00.6 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in this frame?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Looking across the table from the window, on the right-hand side of the window is General Gvero, and then to his left is General Mladic, sort of almost sitting opposite General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Finally, we are pausing at one hour three minutes 5.2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Who do you recognise in this frame, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Moving from the left to the right of the frame is General Mladic on the far left, and then behind him, partially obscured, is Colonel Baxter. In the middle of the frame is myself, and to the right of the frame, with the blue beret on, is General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Who is going first, Defence teams? Okay, Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a cross-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I do not have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I do have a couple of minutes, but I'll defer to my learned friend, if he'd like to go first, or I can just ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is your friend?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They all are, but Mr. Josse is who I'm referring to at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse. You seem to be everybody's friend today. Mr. Thayer referred to you as "my friend," my Ostojic also as his friend. Would you like to go first?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the courtesy is appreciated and much needed today. I would rather not go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I thought so. Mr. Ostojic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. My name is John Ostojic. I represent Mr. Beara in this case. I have a couple of questions that came up from your direct examination that I did not anticipate asking you, so thank you for coming and for answering my questions. You said that in 1998, you spent some time in New York, working specifically on the issue of weapons of mass destruction. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me specifically what your job duties and responsibilities were in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of the question? What's the relevance of the question? What does it change?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking the question, Your Honour, although I'll say it in front of the witness, in connection with the aerial images that we'll be discussing today or tomorrow and her involvement on them, and I think it's important for the credibility of this witness as well as for the other aerial images that the Prosecution is seeking to bring into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our answer is an emphatic "no," Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I proceed and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or are you barring all questions on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course -- we are barring only questions that we see have absolutely no relevance to what we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it may go to credibility, Your Honour, as well, but I'll ask the question and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Credibility, you're asking her what kind of work she did in New York in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To lay the foundation, Your Honour, I was, but I'll proceed and ask a direct question. Thank you, ma'am, and thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in examining and reviewing aerial images in connection with your work with respect to the weapons of mass destruction in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this really is way outside the bounds. Even if it's being proffered to go to credibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I like fishing, Mr. Ostojic, and all fishing expeditions, but I think you have embarked on one which I don't like at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry the Court is not pleased with it, but I don't think it's a fishing exercise, to be quite candid with the Court. I think it's important to show that these aerial images could have been and were from time to time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- manipulated and distorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- we are dealing with some aerial images and not any others, and it was categorically made clear that the way those aerial images were taken, the whole process was not our business. And if that was not our business, I don't see why any other aerial images and madam's expertise or lack of it in relation to aerial images have got any relevance for what we are discussing, so let's move to pastures new.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, ma'am. I hope to get an answer to some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, could you tell me exactly if you could rate the level of knowledge and experience you have with respect to the Serbo-Croatian language as you knew it in 1995?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to my deployment in 1995, I had recently obtained an interpreter-level qualification by the Institute of Linguists in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What level was that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: It's interpreter level -- there are a number of different levels recognised by the institution -- Institute of Linguists, and my piece of paper said that I had passed that interpreter level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there a level above or below that interpreter's level with that institute?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there's one above that will allow you to do simultaneous translation, so I am not sufficiently skilled in Croatian to interpret at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So was the language that you studied specifically Croatian or was it Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: At my university in England, the title of the degree was "Russian and Serbo-Croat," and you had to choose which you were examined in. So I had chosen the Croatian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long was that course study before you passed and got the level that you just shared with us, the interpreter's level?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My degree course was four years, and I did an additional period of study for about two months prior to taking the exam, and that was an intensive course with native speakers in order to improve my translation level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you just strictly conversational, or were you also able to read and write the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I was able to do reading, writing, and conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know, because you studied some Russian, the Cyrillic script as well?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I am proficient in Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have no questions of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, we don't have anything, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci beaucoup, madame. You see, it was a short-lived expectation, but Mr. Haynes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I might as well just get this out of the way. I put no minutes on the schedule, and that's what I meant. I don't wish to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So back to you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ms. Sayers, my name is David Josse, and with the gentleman who sits to my left, we jointly defend General Gvero in this trial, and it won't surprise you to know that I do have quite a number of questions for you, in light of your evidence. We were provided yesterday, very helpfully by Mr. Thayer, with what is called a proofing note, and it gives some background as to how you come to be here today, and I want to explore that with you a little bit, if I may. You received e-mails, as I understand it, from both General Smith and Mr. Dibb in the relatively near past; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's take them in turn, if we may. Firstly, General Smith. Have you been in contact with him regularly or at all in the last ten years?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Over the last ten years, there have been a couple of occasions where we have served in the same location, primarily in Northern Ireland, when I was the adjutant for the Force Intelligence Unit, and I did see him from time to time then when he was the general officer commanding in Northern Ireland. And outside of that, we have met on perhaps two or three separate occasions, certainly in Kosovo when he visited Kosovo, and I was the media -- one of the media officers, and on a couple of social occasions since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many e-mails has he sent you in the last ten years?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Less than -- less than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So this wasn't the only e-mail he has sent you, the one that relates to your being here today?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No. The one prior to that that I had received was him establishing an e-mail contact after my wedding in November. Previous to that, we had lost contact, and a mutual friend attended the wedding and had passed my e-mail address on to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That -- that really deals with my next question, which is how he came to have your e-mail address. That's very helpful, thank you. Let's deal with Mr. Dibb. A similar question. A brief resume of your dealings with him over the last ten years.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: We -- I have met with Captain Dibb on a number of occasions in the last ten years. However, since leaving the army in 2000, they became fewer and fewer, especially after he became involved in his de-mining activities and spent large time -- large lengths of time abroad. But we have in fairly regular e-mail contact, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So when you heard from them, you were not particularly surprised; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Dealing strictly and only with matters pertaining to this case, what did General Smith say to you, please?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Both the e-mails from both of them arrived within a day or so of each other, and I actually received Captain Dibb's first. And General Smith's e-mail said: "I've been asked by the MOD if I know where you are. Do you want to be found?"

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what did General Smith say?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, that was -- that was General Smith. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's my fault. What did Dibb say then, please?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Tom e-mailed that Mr. Thayer had been trying to locate me and also asked if I wanted to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we have heard that the United Kingdom authorities apparently had made sustained efforts in the last two or three months to find you. They don't have your details, is that right, the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I think the Ministry of Defence were slightly confused by my change of surname. I am required, being a member of the regular reserve, to return a form every year, telling them my current address and details, and I do that every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you're still in the reserve, are you?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Every regular officer remains on the reserve until the age of 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It shows you what I know about the British Army. But, anyway, that's my fault. Thank you. And presumably you're in receipt of some sort of pension as well, are you?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm rather too young to be in receipt of pension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm -- I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you talk to either Mr. Dibb or General Smith after you had received their e-mails pertaining to this case?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did they communicate with you further? Presumably, you e-mailed back and said you were prepared to be found or whatever. Did either of them communicate with you further thereafter?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I believe I received e-mails from both of them, saying that they'd passed my contact details on to the -- respectively from Mr. Dibb to Mr. Thayer and from General Smith to an MOD lawyer, and I then directly made contact with the MOD lawyer and directly made contact with Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You made direct contact with Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, using the information that had been given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you had no idea why it was that Mr. Thayer wanted to talk to you at the point you first made contact with him; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: When we were planning -- when I was planning my wedding last autumn, I had made contact with Mr. Dibb to see whether he was going to be in the U.K., and he had mentioned that he wouldn't be in the U.K. because he'd recently been here in The Hague, and that was the extent. So I knew that -- that Tom had been to The Hague to testify in a trial. I didn't know what the trial was, or who was involved, or how long he'd been here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so at the point that you first made contact with Mr. Thayer, you didn't know which of the accused in this case the Office of the Prosecutor were interested in your helping them with?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We were told, in the proofing note, that, and I quote here, and I'll read it out slowly: "Smith stated that he had testified in several trials, and she should not expect people to know exactly how UNPROFOR worked." What did you understand him to mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: When I had had the e-mail conversation around the time of the wedding with Tom, he had -- he had stated that he felt that it wasn't clear how UNPROFOR had operated, and that was the only comment he made. And when I responded to General Smith that I was happy to be found, I must have referenced that in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did he explain it at all?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's my not understanding it. The comment that I've just read out came originally from Mr. Dibb, as I understand what you've said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That is correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You returned that comment, so to speak, to General Smith, or passed it on, in effect; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I may have referenced it in some way, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what I'm asking you is: Did General Smith seek to clarify the remark that you had referenced?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: In the e-mail he sent me that said he'd passed on my details to the MOD lawyer, he made -- there was a sentence that said something like: "It's not ICTY's role to understand how UNPROFOR worked."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what did you understand him to mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That the mechanics of how UNPROFOR operated on the ground were not the sole purpose of ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on, if I may, to Mr. Baxter. We know that he retired from the army relatively recently as a brigadier general. Have you had any dealings with him over the last ten years?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The only time I've met Brigadier Baxter was in Macedonia, where he was employed by the military when I was working for OCE, so that would have been 2000 and -- actually shortly after the Ohrid Agreement. 2002? I don't recall specifically, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any efforts, either by Smith, Dibb, or by the Prosecution in this case, to contact Mr. Baxter recently?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of General Smith or Mr. Dibb trying to contact him, but I believe that the Ministry of Defence were trying to contact him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge as to whether the Ministry of Defence were successful?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You don't. And you don't know whether the Office of the Prosecutor have or have not spoken to him?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about Mr. Dibb, any knowledge as to whether they have -- whether he's been spoken to either by the Ministry of Defence or by the Office of the Prosecutor subsequently about these events?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Could you clarify "subsequently"?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Subsequent to his giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to turn to the approach that you received from the Office of the Prosecutor. You've, in fact, explained very helpfully that it was you who contacted them initially. Presumably, they made it clear to you that they wished to speak to you. Did you have any form of conversation as to the substance of your evidence prior to your meeting in London on, I think, the 25th of January of this year?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I did speak to Mr. Thayer on the telephone prior to the actual interview, just setting up the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll correct myself. It was the 24th of January, the day of the interview. Any discussion as to the substance of your evidence? That's really all I'm curious about.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. So you set up a meeting, and you were interviewed by Mr. Thayer and by an investigator called Mr. Janc, I think, that's J-A-N-C for the record, on the 24th of January of this year; that's right?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I don't have a diary in front of me, but on the Thursday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Take it from me, and I just want to be absolutely clear about this. That was the first time you had any idea as to what anyone was interested in what you had to say about the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: When I arrived at the MOD, I was given a list of questions that had been -- had been sent by the MOD lawyer, and that was the morning of the meeting. I had been sent a packet of documents that arrived on Wednesday, and I'd had a short while to look at some of these documents overnight on the night before the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The documents had come from the Ministry of Defence or from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I believe they came from the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm -- they had a -- I didn't keep the package.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you can't tell us which documents this package included?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I can tell you which documents were included in the package, but I didn't -- I didn't include the -- I didn't keep the envelope is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand. Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: There were a number of meeting reports memorialising meetings over a period of 1995, and they included meetings with Bosnian civilian politicians and the reports that we've reviewed today in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to change the subject. I may come back to what I was asking you about in a few moments' time. Notes that you kept at the time, please. Did you keep any form of diary or notebook of contemporaneous events?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: None whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And subsequently, did you make any attempt or have you made any attempt, perhaps I should say, to write anything about your experiences in Bosnia in 1995?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you undergo any form of debriefing in 1995 after you left Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you clarify what you mean by "debriefing"?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, debriefing presumably by some form of British or perhaps United Nations official, who asked you to tell them anything about your experiences.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: When -- the only experience that I had that may suit that moniker would be every person, when they're serving by themselves, i.e., not attached to a formal unit, and talks to -- gets debriefed by a sort of psychological -- for psychological reasons when they leave theatre. I think it's to make sure that, you know, that you're okay to be sent back to your unit. That was my understanding of its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you these questions is to clarify that the events that you're describing today in court, you have not thought about -- well, correction. You have not discussed with anyone or written down in the 12 years since they've happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And obviously 12 years is quite a lot of time and a lot of water's passed under the bridge. That goes without saying, doesn't it? But I ask you that all the same.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm not really sure what the point of your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay, I'll -- well, the point's neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not exactly neither here nor there, it's -- usually that's the question or the point made to a witness when one is trying to challenge his or her memory. So go ahead, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, yes. But, Your Honour, I don't need to tell the witness why I'm asking a particular question. It wasn't a very good question. That I certainly accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree, so let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Inelegantly and clumsily put.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You, as you told the Trial Chamber, primarily were responsible for dealing with the Muslim side, and Mr. Dibb, I think, was primarily responsible for liaising with the Serb side in the dispute?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And your role in these events was primarily because Mr. Dibb was physically stationed in Zepa for a few days?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you've been asked about your dealings with General Gvero, and I'm not going to ask you specifically about them again, but you are confident that your first meeting with him was on the 25th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Had you had any dealing with him at all prior to that day?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I do believe we had met before that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Had you had any dealing with him, other than face to face, prior to that day? Any telephone conversation with him is specifically what I've got in mind.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That was not normally part of my role, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It wasn't normally part of your role. If a senior UNPROFOR officer needed to speak to an officer of the VRS or, indeed, an officer -- well, let's deal with the VRS for a moment, who would act as a translator for that UNPROFOR officer?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Ordinarily, that would have been Captain Dibb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you translate telephone conversations between senior Bosniaks, civilian or military leaders, and senior UNPROFOR figures?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you did that quite regularly?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: On a fairly regular basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Josse. Just to clarify this from the transcript, at line 6 on the previous page, page 37, your question: "Now, you have been asked about your dealings with General Gvero, and I'm not going to ask you specifically about them again, but you are confident that your first meeting with him was on the 25th of July of 1995?" And Ms. Sayer answered: "Yes, I believe so." Then your question: "Had you had any dealings with him at all prior to that day?" " And her answer is: "I do believe we had met prior to that day," which is contrary to what she had previously stated. My understanding is that prior to the 25th of July, she had never met with General Gvero, but her answer on line 12 indicates exactly the contrary. I don't think she said that or she meant to indicate that she had met with General Gvero before the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that's very beady-eyed of Your Honour, because I certainly hadn't spotted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can clarify. Occasionally there are transcription errors. Is that right, madam?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: May I clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, and please draw a distinction between having met him before and having dealings with him before, because the question itself was not directed as to whether you had met him before but whether you had dealings with him before the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that I had dealings with General Gvero before the 25th of July, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, you can pursue the matter or jump --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to pursue it in one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But just before I do that, as a lead-in to it, could I ask you this: You were based where in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: We were -- I was based with Command of UNPROFOR in a building known as the residency in the center of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so that was not the building that General Gobillard was in; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That is correct, apart from the time that General Gobillard covered for General Smith earlier in that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was the first two weeks of July, wasn't it --

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- approximately? And General Gobillard, was he someone you met?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I did meet General Gobillard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were you present when Generals Gobillard and Smith communicated with one another, spoke to one another?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What language did they use?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: There were -- it would depend at the level of conversation. We worked in a big office, so the liaison officer and interpreters were in a big office outside, and so when General Gobillard came to meet with General Smith, they would greet each other in English and exchange a few words in English, and then the meetings would happen in General Smith's office, and I was not at those meetings. So I can't answer the question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of General Gobillard's military assistant?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I can describe him facially to you, but I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do that.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: He is -- we met again in the UN, when I was working in the UN in New York. He has fairly dark skin and dark eyes, with dark hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What nationality is he?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: He was French.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And at what period of time was this man General Gobillard's military assistant?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the period in -- while I was in Sarajevo. I have no knowledge of any other period other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I'm going to suggest you're wrong about this. His military assistant was a French-Canadian who in fact had fair hair, a man called Fortin, Louis Fortin. Does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the name of General Smith's chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: General Nikolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he was Dutch, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, he was Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What language did you speak to him in?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I spoke to General Nikolai occasionally in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You say "occasionally." Did he not require your interpretive skills?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I never worked with General Nikolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Even though he was based in the residency as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever work with or for General Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The occasion I recall working -- or was really receiving a telephone conversation when General Gobillard was covering for General Smith, and on that occasion I took a -- I recall taking a telephone conversation from Minister Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was that the only conversation that you recall performing that function for Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. Let me come to the point. Let's have a look at P2968, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, this is quite a long document, and I think you may need to read it all, but it purports, when it comes up on the screen, to be a record made by a Major Fortin of a telephone conversation. You have it, I see. We don't. Yes, we've got it now. A telephone conversation between General Gobillard and General Gvero on the 11th of July at 1810 hours. I think it would be advisable were you to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I haven't objected yet to the somewhat wide-ranging nature of the cross-examination. You know, I think my friend ought to be allowed some latitude, given the circumstances. But we are now getting into an area which is a record of a telephone conversation regarding somebody that the witness didn't work with, didn't serve as an interpreter for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- and I'm just concerned we're really moving far afield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but let's wait for the question. What surprises me is that Mr. Josse, for two days or three days running, had complained that he would not have enough time to prepare for his cross-examination, and now he is mounting a really humongous cross-examination. So you found the time, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I found the time, and they teach us to be tough at the English Bar, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. The same in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I say, madam, I think you might need to read this, because I'm going to ask you, in due course, whether you were involved in this conversation at all. So I suspect the only way you might recall this is by reading the substance of it. When you get to the end of that page, say so, and the Registrar will turn the page for you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm at the end of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Having read it, does it ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm afraid it doesn't ring any bells. I don't recollect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you this is: On the 28th of November, in this courtroom, at page 18382 of the transcript, Major Fortin was giving evidence about this conversation, and he said this: "Well, as far as I recall, the interpreter would talk to General Gvero in Serbo-Croatian. He would reply. She would translate to me in English. I would translate to General Gobillard in French. He would give me his reply in French. I would tell it in English to the interpreter, and she would then translate for the person at the other end. "Q. And the interpreter you are referring to is Captain Bliss? "A. I'm quite sure it was Captain Bliss." What do you say about that, please?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is he wrong?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: There -- there were a number of interpreters who spoke Serbo-Croat in the residency at the time. I can't -- I can't say that he was wrong, but I do not have -- all I can comment is that I don't have a recollection of having interpreted this conversation. And ordinarily, when I was involved in an interpretation of a telephone conversation, I made notes, and this is -- does not have the hallmark of my notes. But I believe you said it was created by Mr. Fortin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps that would be a convenient moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before you proceed, I've been informed that Ms. Sayer would like to make a statement in relation to some answer that she has given. Ms. Sayer, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, thank you. I just wanted to clarify. You asked me if I recalled a certain person, and I described the person. The person I described was the MA to a French general but not General Gobillard, and I did realise that when I -- as soon as you responded to me, but I didn't feel that I had the opportunity to comment at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours. So what you're saying, Ms. Sayer, is that the person you described was a military assistant to another French general, not General Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It may have been General Janvier, was it?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: It was General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and we'll try to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My apologies. I will try and speak particularly slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. You usually do, so you're not usually a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a little later about this Major Fortin, as he was at the time. He's now a colonel, and as I say, he gave evidence here in November. You have no recollection of him at all?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I recall when General Gobillard and his team moved in for a very short period earlier that month into the residency, there were lots of new faces, and it had not been part of my role to liaise with Sector Sarajevo before that time, so all of these people were new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll go straight to the point now. I'm going to suggest to you that Major Fortin was in Zepa on the evening of the 27th-28th of July. Is it possible that you weren't aware of UNPROFOR officers who were in Zepa that night?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: On every occasion when we were in Zepa, we stayed at the check-point at the top of the enclave, so it is possible that he was not there, or indeed it's possible that he was there and I don't recall seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll explore that in a moment. But what was that check-point known as, the one that you stayed at?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: OP-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come to that in a moment, if I may. 25th of July, I'd like to turn to first of all. Had you ever been to the Jela Restaurant before, before that day?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: On one occasion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: It's in the region of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Behind you, and don't look at it quite yet, is a very large map of the area, and I'm going to ask you to put various marks on it over the next half an hour or so. If you can, and if you can't, say so, a few places, Zepa, Sokolac, Rogatica, have been highlighted in the map to help, but otherwise it's unmarked. Coincidentally, it's actually a Ministry of Defence -- British Ministry of Defence map dated 1995. Could you mark on that map, please, where you say the Jela Restaurant is? If you can't, say.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can. I wasn't the driver, so -- I'll try. I'm sorry. Beyond being -- beyond saying it's in the region of Sokolac, I would not feel confident in marking it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know why it was chosen as a meeting place?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you get there on that day, the 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: In an UNPROFOR vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: From Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall the route that you took?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't recall the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where was the nearest check-point to the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: On leaving the residency, I recall going through a number of check-points, but I can't recall the exact location of -- of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where was the nearest check-point to the restaurant? If you don't remember, say so.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was in your entourage that day? General Smith's entourage, that is.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I was the interpreter/liaise officer, and I recall Mr. Davidson being the chief bodyguard, and I recall we were in two vehicles and that there were approximately seven or eight of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who, if anyone from the VRS, was there to greet you when you arrived at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My recollection is that General Tolimir was at the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Alone?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: There were other officers or other personnel in uniform around, but I couldn't name them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Gvero arrive there with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm not sure. My recollection is that that is what happened, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did Mladic get to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My understanding was that he came by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was General Gvero in that helicopter with him?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I did not see it land, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mladic was late for the meeting, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It in fact says that in the minute that we looked at earlier. What happened in the 30 minutes that you were waiting for Mladic?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: As was normal, we were offered hospitality in the form of a drink or coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Anything else? Did Tolimir say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't recall the specific nature of any conversations, apart from normal sort of pleasantries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to suggest to you that in fact it was General Gvero who greeted you when the arrived at the Jela Restaurant on the 25th of July, and he started to talk to General Smith about the British political system. He mentioned the House of Commons, the House of Lords, the prime minister. Any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then he mentioned various British philosophers, for example, J.S. Milne, Bertram Russell. Any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, however it is possible that I didn't interpret this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you weren't interpreting, who would, please?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: If I wasn't physically interpreting --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: -- there was normally an interpreter from the Serb side present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any recollection whether there was an interpreter from the Serb side present for that meeting and who that interpreter was?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. They varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: During the actual meeting after Mladic had arrived, did you interpret the substance of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Not on that occasion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you attend the substance of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Gvero say anything during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My major recollection of the time that we were actually at the restaurant centers on the conversation about Bihac, and that primarily occurred between General Smith, who was asking a number of questions and to try to move the conversation on to Bihac, and General Mladic responding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was Tolimir's contribution to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I have no real recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you sure that Tolimir was there?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've got a picture in your mind's eye of General Tolimir being at this meeting, have you?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That is reinforced or was reinforced by my reading of the meeting note.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you have told the Trial Chamber that you went to Zepa on the 25th, the 26th and the 27th of July.
