Has that always been your recollection since you were asked about these events, bearing in mind you've only been asked about it for the last two or three weeks? Has that always been your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That's been my recollection since it happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. We'll turn to that in a moment. Perhaps before I do that, I should have asked you about the 25th of July, Ms. Sayers. We know that Mladic goes off to Zepa, thereafter, he goes in a helicopter; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you do, you personally?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Get into two vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And go where?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Go to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you're in the same vehicle as General Smith, a separate vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The same or a separate vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The same vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where does General Gvero go; any idea?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I go back to what I asked you a minute ago. You are saying that since you were first asked about these events on the 24th of January of -- I beg your pardon -- yes, the 24th of January of this year, you have always maintained you were in Zepa on the 25th, the 26th, and the 27th of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: When I made my statement on the 24th, my recollection -- in fact, it's -- I believe it's in the statement, was that we spent two or three days in Zepa. And then towards the end of the statement, when, after reviewing the meeting notes, because there are some discrepancy on the dates on the notes, it was my recollection that there were three days rather than two to three.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why didn't you say that when I asked you the question two or three minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, two or three minutes ago, and I could go to the question if it would help you, madam, I asked you the following -- I will go to the question: "Now, you've told the Trial Chamber that you went to Zepa on the 25th, 26th, and 27th of July. Had that always been your recollection since you were asked about these events, bearing in mind you've only been asked about it for the last two or three weeks? Had that always been your recollection?" Answer: "That's been my recollection since it happened." That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at your witness statement and see if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to. I'll explain it to the witness. What's being put to you is the following, madam: When you answered the question that Mr. Josse has just read out to you, your answer is tantamount to confirming that your recollection has always been that you were three days in Zepa, the 25th, 26th, and 27th. Mr. Josse is putting to you that that is not correct, because later on you, yourself, referred to your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor whereby at one stage you are not sure whether it was three days, in fact you said "two or three days," and it's only later that you realise that it was three days and not two or three days. So it's being put to you that it's not true, it's not correct, that your recollection has always been uniform and constant, in the sense that it was three days and not something different. This is what is being put. This is what is being put. If I have misinterpreted your position, Mr. Josse, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour hasn't, and I'm going to go to the witness statement, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if the witness could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I thought there was a witness statement coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to explain the apparent discrepancy between your previous answer and what transpires from your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a matter of recall. During the course of the interview that I had with the Prosecution in London, I was asked a number of questions in terms of dates, and I could not recall the exact dates. And when I was originally asked the question, I answered, "Two or three days." Then having reviewed the documents, many of which I authored, parts of those meeting notes, and thinking about it over a -- over a break, I was able to confirm that it was three days rather than two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are, in actual fact, conceding Mr. Josse's proposition that it is not exactly correct when you state that your recollection, ever since the events happened, has always been that you were three days in Zepa, that in other words you came back to realise that it was three days after you were given the opportunity to go deeper into what was being shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, although at the time, that summer, when discussing, you know, with my family, who had obviously seen what was going on on the television, I have said to them, "Oh, yes, it was an interesting three days," so it's -- forgive me -- so, you know, at some level, three, rather than two to three, has been in my mind for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I think you can safely proceed to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the same witness statement, in the next paragraph, and I can show it to you if it would help, I'm going to read paragraph 10 to you: "I recall General Mladic, Tolimir, and Gvero being in Zepa area during this time." And then there is a passage that has been blanked out, which we don't need to worry about. I don't know what it says, and that's been dealt with elsewhere. "I saw General Mladic at the Jela Restaurant, then at the check-point overlooking Zepa. I saw General Gvero at the Jela Restaurant on 25 July and think I may have seen him again that day, passing him on the road, but I'm not sure because these days are difficult to distinguish." And I'll finish the paragraph: "I recall seeing General Tolimir with Tom Dibb and Colonel Coiffet at the check-point in Zepa on 25 July." Nothing in your evidence hitherto, Ms. Sayers, about "these days are difficult to distinguish." Why not?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My evidence to the questions you've asked me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Thayer asked you, more to the point. You didn't tell this Trial Chamber, "Well, to be honest with you, these days are difficult to distinguish. I'm not sure if there were two or three days." You've come in here and you've given the clear impression that you're absolutely confident in what you said. It's different to what your witness statement says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it is different, I suppose, but I would like to clarify that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's why I'm giving you an opportunity to do exactly that. Please clarify it.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That I hadn't seen any written evidence relating to that time for the last 12 years, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the packet that you received the day before?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Well, obviously until that time, as I've explained already today, I received the packet of documents that was provided to me the day before I met with Mr. Thayer and his colleague in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let there be no doubt about it. You received this packet before you wrote this witness statement, before you said the days were difficult to distinguish. What changed subsequently for you to say that the days are no longer difficult to distinguish?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My memory has not been exposed to any questioning since these things happened, and I have not thought, you know, in any great way about the events, so in my opinion there is a level of clarity that comes with giving a level of thought and examination to the memories in one's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is your evidence at this moment in time that the days are difficult to distinguish?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: As I -- as I said earlier, I'm quite clear in my mind now that there were three visits to Zepa on the days that we have discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you didn't ever go into Zepa town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did you remain?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: At the check-point at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Because my role was to stay with General Smith and be of use when I was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He went into the town on occasions?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I did not accompany him in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next question with the map: Are you able to indicate approximately, looking at the map, where the enclave boundary is? Would you be able to draw an approximate line 'round Zepa as to where the safe area was?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I should clarify, I've never seen an unmarked map before, so I'm not sure I would get it in the right place. Not with any confidence, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I'll come back to that in a moment. Can you mark where you say the check-point was, OP-2; in other words, where you remained whilst Smith did his business in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, sorry to interrupt you, but where does it get you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it going to change anything? The check-point has always been where it has been, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm anxious to test --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it important to know whether the witness knows the exact location of the check-point and pinpoint it with precision on the map or without precision on the map? What is it going to change if she doesn't know the boundaries or if she doesn't know the exact location?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm certainly not going to persist, Your Honour, and if the witness doesn't know, I'm quite content to accept that answer. But as is apparent, I'm testing her recollection of all these events as best I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the only armoury I have in my possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that, but again these are petty issues which have very little bearing at all as to recollection, because they are topographical things and she's already made that clear. She was driven there, she's never seen an unmarked map, so it's all complicated to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before I move to the 27th of July, one other thing I'd like to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have an assistant here, you've got help. Yes, General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I need a leader.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] With all due respect for the Court, I wanted to say, and with the full respect for the witness, that the witness has been repeating for the umpteenth time that she was in Zepa for three days. Since the control or check-point was not in Zepa and it was not in the protected area of Zepa, I believe it is important to note that fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Josse is thankful for that observation and that he will take it into consideration in his next questions. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before we turn to the check-point situation within the enclave itself, I just want to go back to the part of your witness statement that I read to you about the 25th of July. The relevant bit is as follows: "I saw General Gvero at the Jela Restaurant on 25 July and think I may have seen him again that day, passing him on the road, but I'm not sure because these days are difficult to distinguish." What did you mean when you say that you may have passed him again on the road? What's your recollection about that, please?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My recollection is that on driving to the check-point and coming out to the check-point, there was quite a lot of traffic. There were numerous vehicles that we passed. And the point I was making is that I may have seen him in one of these vehicles, but I could not be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which check-point are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I was referring to our journey from the Jela Restaurant to Zepa, to the place that I have described as the check-point OP-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you're referring again to OP-2, are you?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you are saying that in your estimation, there's a chance that you saw Gvero again in the Zepa area after the Jela Restaurant meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: That's -- that's my belief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How high would you place that possibility?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: In comparison to my certainty of seeing him on the 27th, it is not as strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And there was no conversation on the 25th of July, if you saw him at all; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: There wasn't -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think I've already asked you this, but you do not recall how he left the meeting at the Jela Restaurant, what mode of transport he took?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I believe you have asked that before, and I don't -- I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I want to suggest he didn't get into the helicopter with Mladic, he eventually got into a car. It may have been you'd left by then, but he didn't get into the helicopter, did he?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: As I have said twice now, I -- I don't recall seeing how General Gvero departed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When -- this encounter you're not sure about at OP-2 on the 25th of July, what car was Gvero in?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I didn't say it was at OP-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've misunderstood you, then. Where was it?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: It may have -- my recollection is that it was en route, not necessarily at the OP-2 check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to help us at all as to whereabouts on the route it was?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- I was just a passenger in those vehicles. I -- I couldn't give any certainty as to where it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You don't know how near or far from the boundary of the enclave this encounter on the 25th of July was; is that what --

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment. I think it would be easier if you had a look at your witness statement for the next set of questions. Your Honour, it's not been put into e-court, but we've got a copy for the ELMO and indeed one for the witness as well so she's got a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've also got a few B/C/S copies which have been provided by the Prosecution, which we thought could be shared amongst the accused in the dock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I wasn't -- they weren't intended for the Bench. They were intended for the accused, because it's not in e-court and therefore they won't be able to follow it in their own language. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had they been in e-court, we would have been able to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So I provided you with your own copy there, Ms. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There we are. It's paragraph 12 that I want to concentrate on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see that it begins: "You asked me if I recall stopping at a check-point in the Zepa area on my last day there and seeing a nice car." What happened during your meeting, so far as this was concerned? Why have you used the words "you asked me if I recall"?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Because I was responding to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In other words, you didn't volunteer the information; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I was -- I believe I was responding to a question about, "Describe what happened on your final day in Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, in terms of the chronology of the witness statement, goes after the bit that I have read relating to the 25th of July; in other words, you had volunteered that encounter?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I responded to questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there any reason why it says: "You asked me if I recall ..."?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the use of the words "check-point in the Zepa area on my last day there and seeing a nice car"; in other words, that idea had to be put into your head, you didn't volunteer that information? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I recall the term "a nice car" being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you volunteer the information prior to being asked this leading question? That's really what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My recollection is that we had had quite a long conversation or interview about this period, and I'd been asked to -- some specific questions on the different reports that are identified, and then a number of questions testing -- testing my recollection of the period were asked to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because of course the reports don't help at all on the encounter with Gvero, do they?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, they're not minuted in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in fact the reports don't really take the main reason you're here, which is to describe this encounter, one jot further, do they? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The reports are what they are. They're a record of -- of events as they were recorded at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the check-point you're referring to is which one?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: As we were leaving Zepa, there are a number of times where we would stop or be waved through as we're coming on the very long journey back to Sarajevo. My recollection is that it took a good time. You know, hours were spent travelling on those days, and indeed on the first day, it was a very late evening because of the amount of time it had taken us to travel back before we then met with people at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which check-point are you referring to in the first sentence of paragraph 12, if you know?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the check-point. In fact, I don't -- other than "OP-2," I don't know the names of any of the check-points on what was then BSA territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was not OP-2; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know whether this check-point was in fact within the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I can't say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It may not have been?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: It was on the road from Zepa back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By all means, have a look at the map behind you. It may help. It's extremely detailed. And see if that helps your recollection as to where this check-point was.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't be certain where the check-point is. I recall the route back being through an area with lots of trees, and one of the -- at this check-point is where I remember it being.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just want to see if I understand what you're saying, Ms. Sayer, in the answer you gave at the beginning of page 62 of our transcript of today. You described travelling for a long period. Of course, this was a day trip from Sarajevo to Zepa and then back again. Are you saying that it was a long time after leaving Zepa that you had this encounter with Gvero on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How long had you been travelling after you had the encounter with Gvero?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: It would be hard for me to be specific, but I would say, you know, 20, 30 minutes, maybe. It was relatively -- relatively soon after we left check-point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where -- I think you've said your recollection is that General Smith didn't come out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I have no clear recollection of him actually leaving the vehicle, because it -- because of a security situation. The bodyguards didn't -- weren't very comfortable with -- with the principal getting out of the vehicle when we were between places. It was not the common practice at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your witness statement, which you've got in front of you, paragraph 12 still, about five lines up, says: "I believe that General Smith was a party to the conversation, possibly speaking through an open door at his vehicle." Why did you use the word "believe" and "possibly"?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Because of the stature of General Gvero, it wouldn't have been very -- it wouldn't have accorded with our protocol for me to be having a direct conversation with him. I would be, you know, the conduit for the conversation between the generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, it's common ground that you, in common with all other UNPROFOR personnel, made no record whatsoever of this encounter. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, in the witness statement, you say that had you heard Gvero say that he was taking command or charge, you would have put it in the report. And then you go on to explain that because they were the three busiest days of your deployment, not everything made it into an official record. What was it that would have been significant about him saying that he was in charge to merit that going in a report, rather than the encounter itself?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: The reports that we wrote, the meeting notes, they were solely designed as a summary, and you will, I hope, appreciate that over the course of these days, there were many interactions between a variety of different people, and the primary ones were summarised, what we thought to be salient facts at the time, so that they could then be recorded and sent up to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so a salient fact would have been a senior officer saying he was taking charge, but the actual encounter wouldn't have been sufficiently salient; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that would be a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you base that on the instructions that you had received over the time you had been working with General Smith as to what should and shouldn't go in the report?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yeah, there was an aspiration that we would be as accurate as possible in all of our note-taking, but there was an acceptance that when things were moving at a very fast pace, that we would have to make choices about what was recorded and what wasn't. Otherwise, the meeting note summaries would be 15 pages' long. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I don't want to belabour this point, but you are saying that you have no real idea where, in relation to Zepa, this encounter took place; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My -- I'm not sure it's totally fair, no, because my recollection is that we were on the road from check-point 2 back to Sarajevo, and it happened in a fairly short period in comparison to the length of the journey back to Sarajevo, after our departure from check-point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me try it one other way. Had you passed Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, I don't believe we had passed Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Definitely not?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. The 31st of July, you have told the Chamber that you again saw my client, and you have described him talking about scything?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did he mention anything else to you that sticks in your memory? Again, Mladic -- let me start again. Mladic was late, wasn't he, yet again?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. General Smith was preoccupied, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I would have said General Smith was angry rather than preoccupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, he was angry. He was angry because someone had taken a shot at the helicopter that you were in?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Actually, several shots, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. And he made that plain to Gvero, did he?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The interaction was fairly heated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And at some point, General Gvero mentioned the scything. Did he also mention that in fact he was a local of Mrkonjic Grad and had particular local knowledge; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I believe that's how we got on to the subject of scything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm curious. Tell me if this is a false or bad point, but when you were asked about this by Mr. Thayer a little time ago, at page 19, line 14 of the transcript, you were asked by Mr. Thayer: "And do you recall General Gvero being present for this meeting?" And you said: "Yes, I -- I clearly recall General Gvero being present." Why did you use the word "clearly" there?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Because there's no -- there's no doubt in my mind that General Gvero was there, and because this was one of the very few occasions where I was called upon to act as the primary interpreter for this meeting, and hence my -- my issue with the word for size. You know, it was not something that I had come across before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have any awareness as to what Gvero's case is in relation to these various meetings; in other words, has anyone said to you Gvero accepts he was at this meeting but not at that meeting; do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: There's been no conversation in that regard at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So have you no idea?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before I put General Gvero's case to you in a moments time, does the name Rajko Kusic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nothing at all. So it clearly follows from that you wouldn't be able to describe Rajko Kusic and you wouldn't know whether you'd had an encounter with him?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: As I explained, it wasn't common practice for me to have these interactions with the BSA officers, so outside, you know, the very few officers I was personally introduced to, I have very little knowledge of who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me be plain, Ms. Sayer. General Gvero accepts that he was at the meeting on the 25th of July in the Jela Restaurant and the 31st of July in Mrkonjic Grad. He does not accept that he had an encounter with General Smith at the check-point on the 27th of July. That's the day -- that's the day you placed it. Can I be clear about that? You're saying it was definitely the 27th of July; you're now sure about that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I am, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you're sure about that for what reason, the date?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Because the final day that I was in -- at check-point -- at OP-2 was the final day we had the conversation with the War Presidency, and it was on that occasion, on our route back into Sarajevo, which was the final time that I made that journey, that this interaction and meeting at this particular check-point with General Gvero occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And one or two questions about what General Smith did immediately prior to leaving Zepa. You wouldn't know, is that right, because you were not with him? You stayed at OP-2 and he went about doing whatever he did in Zepa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: My recollection is that because Tom Dibb was on the ground with Colonel Coiffet, there was a distinction between what we were asked to do at check-point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you leave check-point 2?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: To go into Zepa itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like you to have a look, please, at 6D155.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we pause for a moment? We'll need to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And before it's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. We are back in open session. Mr. Josse has just finished his cross-examination. Mr. Thayer, I understand you have a few questions on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, ma'am. Do you recall the names of any female interpreters who were on staff at UNPROFOR BiH headquarters in Sarajevo or at Sector Sarajevo; do you recall the names of any female interpreters, if any, that were employed during your period of service there?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I can't recall names, but there was an interpreter pool, and there were British military interpreters as well as locally-employed civilians who were within the interpreter pool. So there was certainly education-core related, U.K. military personnel, who acted as interpreters for a range of staff within the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There were some questions about the documents that you received from the Office of the Prosecutor, and received the day before our meeting. Do you have that packet with you, by any chance, here at the witness box or not?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: It's not with me here, but it is in the support room.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, with the assistance of Madam Usher, I just want to show you a packet of materials. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the intention to prove that these are the same documents that she received from MOD?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we do have a couple more minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think the safer way of going about it is to give her an opportunity to go to the room, fetch them, and we can have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we have the time, Mr. President, that would be my preference as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I think that's the way we should go about it. Don't you agree? All right. So, madam, we are giving you sufficient time -- the usher knows where they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, she does. Thank you. These are the documents, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who wishes to have a look at them? I suppose there is nothing about aerial imagery and weapons of mass destruction, so Mr. Ostojic probably won't show an interest, but Mr. Josse probably will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I'm more than happy for the re-examination to proceed, particularly if Mr. Thayer is going to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Okay. In the meantime, could you hand them over to Mr. Josse, and you proceed with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you remember the approximate time frame that the reports contained in that packet covered?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. They cover a time frame from sort of May through to the end of -- end of July, that sort of time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember the nature of the meetings that they memorialised, in terms of who these meetings were with, for example?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. There are a number of meetings that I was able to say categorically that I didn't attend, and there are a number of meetings that I was able to say categorically that I did attend, and I remember drafting or authoring the minutes that were included in the packet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not these reports included meetings with both Bosnian Muslim as well as Bosnian Serb officials and officers?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Yes. There were a range of meetings, including meetings with Dr. Ganic and Prime Minister Silajdzic, and meetings with President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how many tabs are there? In other words, how many reports were included in that -- in that packet?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: Thirty-three.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how long would you say that you were able to spend reviewing those reports before we actually sat down and spoke on the 24th of January?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I received them on the Wednesday morning at our head office in London on my way to a training session that lasted all day, so I first was able to open the packet at 7.30 that evening, and I'm able to be quite precise, because when I returned to my car at the railway station, the battery was flat and I actually read the majority of these documents by the light of a street lamp while I was sitting in the car, waiting for the RAC to turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You can submit that bill to the OTP and we'll try to take care of it. Now, the -- and forgive me, I think I failed to ask you: How are you employed now? You mentioned your head office, and if you would, just tell the Trial Chamber what you do for a living now.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I work for the Heritage Lottery Fund, and I run their regional office in the East Midlands. We give out grants to heritage projects across the U.K.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not, in any of the communications that you had prior to our meeting, whether from General Smith, Mr. Captain Dibb, representatives from the U.K. Foreign Office or MOD, or in any of the conversation -- or in the conversation that you and I had before we met on the 24th of January, was there any mention of any specific person, individual, officer, mentioned to you at any time during any of those contacts?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about in the questions that were given to you by the MOD?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: No, and I actually have the list of questions with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. That will be my last -- second-to-last question. If you could put those up on the ELMO, we'll just take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before they're put on the ELMO, might we have an opportunity to look at these? They've been -- they weren't disclosed. I appreciate that my questions allow this line of re-examination, but there again they weren't -- they weren't disclosed in any form prior to my asking the questions. My questions were speculative. Perhaps I could have a look at them and then decide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see no reason for any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have a couple of extra copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And my understanding is, Mr. Thayer, that these were provided by you to MOD -- MOD or MOD's counsel, upon their request, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, upon their demand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would have understood it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually only received the questions half an hour before I met with Mr. Thayer and his colleague. The MOD gave them to me when I arrived for the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes. Can we have them on the ELMO, please, Madam Usher. Yes, we have them on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be helpful, sir, if I explain that the MOD's printer doesn't allow for any Serbo-Croatian marks, so that's why there's -- "Zepa" is actually rather bizarrely spelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think -- well, I'll just put it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see any reference in this document to any particular individuals, by name, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need to ask the question, because the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yeah, and I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're happy for this to be admitted into evidence in due course and be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That suffices for my purposes, Mr. President. I just have one final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you were asked some questions by my friend, challenging the clarity of certain of your recollections of these events. How would you compare the clarity of your recollection of the discussion you had with General Gvero about scything to the clarity of your recollection of encountering General Gvero at this check-point some, you said, 20 minutes outside of check-point 2?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER
utterances.text: I would say they are at the same level.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any questions, Judge Prost? Judge Stole? Madam, you'll be glad to hear that your ordeal is over. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over at such a short notice, and on behalf of everyone I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, all the exhibits on our exhibit list distributed are already in evidence, with the exception of this list of proposed questions which just became an issue. We have given that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think it never became an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. We have given that the number 3247, and we can have that uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? No objections. They are so admitted. Mr. Josse, would you like to tender any exhibits or documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We didn't use any documents that hadn't hitherto been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not even the markings on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I of course haven't -- thank you for reminding me, and indeed I got a helpful message from one of the Court staff about that a moment ago. I don't mind having a look at it. I haven't really had a chance to examine the mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither have we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm told that apparently she didn't make any markings at the end of the day, but please feel free to approach the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, she clearly didn't mark the map. I'm slightly astonished, because I rather thought she had, but she hadn't. It's a map that therefore has no value at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And there are no further documents that you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. That concludes Emma Sayer's testimony. I propose we have the break now, and then could I invite you to make an effort -- there's a lot to discuss, but could I invite you to make an effort to try to finish today, rather than have to come again tomorrow. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try to move. I propose to deal first with the exhibits relating to Witness Butler. The understanding is the following: That having gone through the Defence motion, we will not be dealing today with 65 ter number 685 and 686, which are the subject of that motion. We'll be dealing with the rest. There is a whole list of Prosecution documents proposed to be tendered. Are there any objections, or do you wish to make a review of them or explain them, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. President. I believe I went over all of them or made reference to a big bunch that Ms. Fauveau has agreed to come in, so I don't think there's any -- any particular issues that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right, let's see if there are. Any objections to the proposed list, with the exception barring those two? Yesterday, I got the impression that Mr. Bourgon mentioned three, but going through the motion, I can only decipher two. If I am wrong, please correct me. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, first I want to sincerely apologise if you felt that my questions with the last witness were inappropriate, but we'll address that at the proper time when we address that specific issue. Thank you. With respect to, I think the third category of documents, it was very difficult to get a handle on it at such a late stage. That would have been -- since we're only objecting to the two narratives, as set out in our motion, we feel that the exhibits that are only included in the brigade, corps, and Main Staff analysis that Mr. Butler did should be acceptable. The documents that are not in those three exhibits, but are included in the narratives that we object to, should be excluded as documents as well. We tried, although we had our hands full on many other issues, as the Court will hear, when we make another application, so that's our general position on this third group of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're trying to work it out with the Prosecution to see if some, like Ms. Fauveau, would like some of the documents in or has no objection and will pass on those, but that's in essence what the third grouping was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. So I notice Mr. Lazarevic. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Borovcanin Defence has an objection to the admission of Document Number 92, 65 ter number 92 from the Prosecution list, on the grounds of a lack of probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is it? I have 91, but I have not seen 92. After 91, there is 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was used in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it should be on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's on page 10 of the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes, yes, okay, all right, I see it now. Okay, yes. You are objecting to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We object on the grounds of lack of probative value of this document, and having in mind the provisions of Rule 89(c). It states that: "The Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." So it is actually also a question of admissibility, not just the question of weight that the Trial Chamber should give to certain evidence. And what we would like to say in our submission, that having in mind that this document is not complete, which we established through cross-examination of Mr. Butler, and had -- that the signature on the document is not by Mr. Borovcanin, it does not have a sufficient probative value to be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 98(c).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm really shocked at that. I thought we had a stipulation about that document. That was one of the reasons why we did not call Mr. Vasic. I made the stipulation on the record. However, given that they've withdrawn from that, the document should come in as -- anyway. They opened the door by questioning Mr. Butler quite a bit about the various units and the various dates related to Mr. Borovcanin. Mr. Butler talked about this document, had reviewed it. It was received from Mr. Vasic as a document from Mr. Borovcanin. The document explains the various dates, the various units, and the door was opened by them. And even if they're going back on what I believe was an agreement, the door is wide open, it should come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't say that Mr. McCloskey was not entitled to use this document in re-examination of Mr. Butler. However, what we agreed upon is that it was not signed by Mr. Borovcanin, it was not dated, and everything -- all the questions that I posed to Mr. Butler, that's what we agreed upon this document. So we don't believe that this document, the way it is, is admissible under Rule 89(c).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But isn't that sufficient reason why it should precisely be in the record? I mean, we are definitely not on the same wavelength on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. We talked about it, we agreed about things about it so that you would be able to understand it and fully gauge it, its problems, its pros, and that's what we had an agreement about, so that now they don't want it in is a big shock to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is as follows, Mr. Lazarevic and

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We think that ultimately, since this document was used during the re-examination, and itself is relevant, we also believe that you cannot rule out probative value the way you have suggested, Mr. Lazarevic. Basically, we look at your objection more in the context of weight that needs to be given to this document, if at all, and that will be a matter to be decided later on. In the meantime, it will be admitted. Any further objections? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Chamber, I suspect, is not going to like, yet again, what I've got to say, because it fits in with the helpful e-mail that we received from Your Honour's senior legal officer earlier today, because 1059 on this list, at page 5, and 45, which is the first document on Mr. Coven's list are of course one and the same. Your Honour, the truth of the matter is the Gvero team have not had time to decide on our submissions in relation to 45 and 1059. 45 was marked for identification originally, I recall, and I suspect 1059 as well, because we challenged the provenance. So the first issue, of course, is the Prosecution need to answer the provenance question. But -- sorry, I haven't put this very clearly, because in fact I have been able to address, in the last minute, 45 and 1059, which I repeat are identical. Perhaps we can then turn to the remaining documents on Mr. Coven's list at a moments time. So the questions is provenance in short so far as that's concerned. There is one other document. Should I deal with that while I'm on my feet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That is at page 12 on the list, and it's 3810, and it's the article allegedly authored by my client called "Silk Cord Alija" part of which Mr. McCloskey read out with such relish last Friday. We suggest that's been introduced for prejudice and prejudice only. The date, being the 15th of July, 1993, is highly significant, highly significant, inasmuch as it goes to the prejudice. It's way outside the indictment period. The witness knew nothing about it, as such. He was asked, in effect, if it was illustrative of my client's role, views on morale, propaganda, so on and so forth, and that sort of pejorative and unfair prosecuting should not be countenanced by this Trial Chamber. We do not object to the other documents used in the re-examination that pertain to our client, but we do object to this particular document, because Mr. McCloskey has put it there for one reason only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please refresh my memory. Did you object at the time this document was used, and was the objection decided?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I did object, on recollection, but I've got it right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I specifically recall the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but if there was an objection, it was definitely decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't leave them in the air, hanging in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I help with the page? It's page 20976 of the transcript. I objected, Mr. McCloskey responded, and the Trial Chamber, after conferring, said, Your Honour -- the learned Presiding Judge said: "Go ahead. Have you finished your question?" So, in short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had turned down the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You turned down the objection. Of course, whilst that may lend some weight to the suggestion the document should be introduced into evidence, it doesn't follow, bearing in mind the nature of the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me confer with my colleagues for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. My apologies to you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to remind you of the situation, he objected that it was beyond the scope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Scope of the indictment, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I had to read back to you his questions, where he was grilling Mr. Butler on the difference between morale and propaganda, and hammering Mr. Butler that he paid way too much attention to propaganda. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we had a morale document drafted by him, and then we had what we believe was a propaganda document drafted by him, and this document is extremely important for this case. This document would be admissible in this case against any accused in a joint criminal enterprise like this, because it shows what we believe is clear, unadulterated racism. And if they call that prejudice, it's not legal prejudice. It certainly harms their case, but it's not legal prejudice. It's our case that this shows the propaganda side of things directly in response to the cross-examination. This document would be admissible under any -- against any of these accused in this case, where we have genocide and we have persecutions and we have racism as a key element in many of these charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In relation to 1059, Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to respond? Basically, Mr. Josse has limited it to the question of provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 1059, are we talking, I believe, about the somewhat famous 13 July order by General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I can tell you that we have received two different versions of this document over the years. I don't have, you know, all the details, but I can tell you that this was -- this document first came to light in the Krstic case and was provided to us by Nenad Petrusic. It's my understanding he got it through the RS government based on a request. He may be able to help me out on that. And we also received it -- it was one of -- I believe one of the documents that Dragan Obrenovic provided early on in the investigation, when he took those documents from the archive that was in Mali Zvornik. And so it comes from two different places, and that's its origins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the other one already admitted, 49?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 45 is not admitted. Exactly the same, marked for identification. Your Honour, could I respond to both of those?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm having a bad day. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We all are, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Dealing firstly with 3180, I didn't object, when one looks at 2976, on the basis of the scope of the indictment. I objected on the basis that my cross-examination went to a different emphasis. Your Honour, at no time did I cross-examine Mr. Butler on the question of racism, or my client's intent, or anything of that sort. If this document is as important as my learned friend suggests, why wasn't it introduced in his case in chief? Why is it being used in this way at the last moment? That's the question the Court needs to ask itself. Is it admissible pursuant to the cross-examination? Where does it take matters? But, really, what he just said, in my submission, gives the game away, because what he said would support the proposition it should be a primary piece of evidence, not something used in re-examination in its very limited way. I mean, it's a fairly limited avenue of the case that it was introduced in re-examination, and now Mr. McCloskey, and I'm sure all of us defending are going to be aware of this from now on, is trying to open the ambit enormously in relation to a document like that. So far as the other document is concerned, 1059, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you know, we've been here for a long time --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry for the interruption. We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've dealt with hundreds and hundreds of god knows how many documents, and every once in a while the Defence objects to one, and most of the time it finds a way of that objection being withdrawn. If we do have just a couple of documents that are really in issue here that they want to hear from witnesses on, we're of course ready to do that, but we're not in the Old Bailey. I can provide the Prosecution's authentication as well as anybody can, and I think we have a document that identifies the source of all Mr. Butler's exhibits, whether they be the Drina Corps collection, the Zvornik collection, or Mr. Petrusic, or somewhere else, and that's just based on, you know, administrative work, and I don't think that's anything that should be a problem. If there's a real issue about something, sure, we can litigate it, and we'll try to avoid calling Mr. Petrusic. I don't think we need to. I think we agree how that came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the last one, 3180. Having heard both of you, we come to the conclusion that in light of the circumstances during which this document was used, leaving apart the question of importance and weight which should or should not be attributed to it, it needs to be admitted. In relation to 1059 and, at the same time, 45, I don't see us finishing today everything that I have to deal with, so what I suggest is that you meet and come to a conclusion, and we'll reach a decision on that tomorrow, based on whether there is an agreement amongst you or whether there's nothing, but I would suggest that you have a look at the transcript which I have here in front of me of the sitting of the 1st of June, 2007, to which I refer you. I think we are in a position to reach a decision now, but we would prefer if you sit down around the table and discuss first amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay, and we are grateful for that. That is really what we are after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further objections to -- have we decided yours, Mr. Lazarevic? Yes, we have. Any further objections? None. We come to the Miletic Defence list. Are there any objections on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has number 18, that's P2891, been translated in the same -- and 20, I don't -- and 20, have they been translated into English or don't they need to be? Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, they are not translated. Those are the documents of the Prosecution, so even if I have to translate them myself, I would need the assistance of the Prosecution to put them on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I notice that 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, are also not translated, so those will be MFI'd, pending translation thereof. Do you wish to comment on the translation issues in relation to 18 and 20, Mr. McCloskey, or not? Should we MFI those as well or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Anything that's not translated will -- a joint request to CLSS to fix.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I also notice that 5D659 doesn't seem to have the corresponding translation in B/C/S, but I would imagine that it exists in B/C/S. Madame Fauveau. We're talking of the law --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have a technical problem which I have to see with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same with 13, 14 and 15, according to the list provided by you, there doesn't seem to be a corresponding B/C/S translation thereof. So the position, Registrar, is as follows: Please check this list with the parties, and wherever there is a translation pending, that document or those documents will be marked for identification, pending translation thereof. All right. Where there is agreement between the parties that there is no need to wait for a translation, then they will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's deal with the Gvero Defence team list. Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Josse, you have just got two documents, 6D223 and 227?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about 227? This is a list of selected terms from the military lexicon. Does that need to be translated or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it doesn't, because 223 translates it, so to speak, and 227 is not an original document, but it's required --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a selection that you made, yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's required to make sense of the transcript, simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. These are admitted. The Nikolic Defence team have got an updated list which has arrived just now. We're talking of six documents, 65 ter number of which appears on the list itself. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note we've got an e-mail from me to everyone regarding -- I think I was telling them the collections and documents Mr. Butler had had a chance to review. I -- it wasn't mentioned in the cross or direct, and I don't see it's a real problem, but I just don't understand what the relevance of it is. These sorts of e-mails are normally something that if I knew they were going to be in court, I would have written it a little differently, but I don't -- I don't know, it may be a Mr. Bourgon issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you insist on this document, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe that we have the total of eight documents on the list. That's why I rose before Mr. McCloskey. I believe that this list contains documents 333A and B or else the confirmation of the indictment from Bosnia-Herzegovina. My colleagues tell me now that they haven't received it. This is an issue that I discussed over the break with Mr. Thayer. As far as 3D274 is concerned, that's a letter that Mr. McCloskey sent in relation to Mr. Butler's contacts with some witnesses, and it concerns certain documents. That's 3D274 I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's still -- okay. So my suggestion is, if you agree, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Nikolic, I remember quite vividly a reference to an e-mail allegedly sent by you to the parties, and I think I can remember also Mr. Bourgon either mentioning it directly to you or putting a question, in the sense that names were mentioned in this e-mail that you had -- that they had received from you. Can anyone refresh our memory on this or refer us specifically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: What I'd particularly like to know is was it used with the witness, not whether or not it was used in the course of some arguments or presentations, but was it used with Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't remember it being used, but I would go to your recollection on that, although you've got me a bit disoriented with the change of people. I've been looking at the same group here for so many months that I -- it's done something to my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will double-check this, but I do believe it was used with the witness. I will go through the transcript once more just to double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We leave this also for tomorrow. All right. The rest of the documents, and the understanding is that there is also 3D133A and B in addition to 3D133. Now, 3D133, I have an indication "MFI." Has it been used before and MFI'd? What do you mean by that, Ms. Nikolic? In the list that you provided, in the column 65 ter number, under "3D133," you have "MFI" in brackets.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was just in touch with my team. We modified the list because in the meantime we received additional information concerning document 3D133. The documents which are supposed to confirm the authenticity of 3D133 are documents now numbered 133A and B, and these are confirmations of the indictment from the Court of BiH in the case Bozic et al. I believe this was touched upon on a number of occasions during cross-examination. Mr. Thayer, I believe, is aware of this. In the meantime, we managed to obtain the document from the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with the indictment. I think I remember that being used. But I hear mention of confirmation materials, and that gets us into a whole another area that I'm not aware of, so I would be reluctant, unless we hear more information on what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. It may have been a misinterpretation. It's not the supporting material with the indictment, confirming the indictment, it's a formal document whereby the Office of the Prosecutor of the BiH confirms that this indictment had been issued by their office. So this is just a formal way of confirming the authenticity of the document issued by the agency giving that confirmation. So there's nothing -- no -- we don't have any material that would go to modify the essentials of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just an indictment, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's just an indictment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the understanding is, as regards the e-mail correspondence, you're going to -- we're going to postpone that until tomorrow. The other one goes in, is admitted. I have the Borovcanin Defence team. I have a list of five documents. Again, please, Mr. Registrar, check with the party, questions of translation, because, for example, with number 4, the translation is pending. Any objection, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these documents are admitted. We come to 7D, that's the Pandurevic Defence team. I have a list of ten documents. Correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will not correct you, because you're not wrong. I simply want to speak to the document in two respects. The first named document, P181, has already been admitted as part of the Prosecution list, so can be deleted. 7D480 is, for some reason in the comments margin, MFI'd. There is absolutely no reason for that at all. It is translated, and Mr. Butler was cross-examined on the English version of it. So that's an error. So the other nine documents I would ask be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your comments, Mr. McCloskey. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see the OTP interview of Milan Maric. I believe that's the subject of a 92 quater motion. If that will simplify it, I'll knock off one extra workload for everybody and not object to that. And if I could just take a look at -- oh, I guess we went -- we were asking for his interview with the OTP -- sorry, his testimony from the Blagojevic trial. So if I could take a look a little more closely at the Milan Maric statement and the statement of Sabic, Vejiz, since we're going to be here tomorrow, I would have a better answer for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Haynes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll sort that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So we'll postpone these two until tomorrow or for tomorrow. The rest is admitted. So now let's get to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the Popovic Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This was first on 31st of January, and it was confirmed, but the title is wrong, because it is said this was the documents for potential use during cross-examination, and it is a mistake. It is -- these are the documents for tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice that several of them are not yet translated. But apart from that, do you have any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So these are all admitted. However, those which are still -- which still require translation will be MFI'd. Now, let's start with several other pending matters. We have, as you know, received the Defence motion relating to the Butler narratives to which I referred earlier on. We've discussed briefly amongst ourselves and came to the conclusion that this definitely needs to be decided before we embark on the Rule 98 bis submissions. You need to know where you stand. So we are cutting down -- reducing the time limit which will be available to you, Mr. McCloskey, to file your response, and we will require that by not later than Monday noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's -- let me start cancelling, myself, now. There is also pending a motion seeking certification from our decision to admit the 18 Prosecution witnesses under Rule 92 bis. It's not our intention to decide it prior to the Rule 98 bis process. It will be decided in due course whenever we are ready to decide it. So for all intents and purposes, our decision stands. That's also according to the Rules, even though there is a request for certification, and you need to keep these 18 witnesses in mind when you make your submissions, if they are relevant at all for the purpose of Rule 98 bis submissions. Now, earlier on today, I signed the decision on the Defence motion requesting removal of Momir Nikolic's statement of fact and acceptance of responsibility from the evidence filed on 30th November 2007. I suppose you are aware of this, so that disposes of the matter. There is also another motion pending which seeks certification to appeal the Trial Chamber's decision to strike the testimony of PW-168, filed on January 2008. We would like you, Mr. McCloskey, to file your response to this motion as early as possible, possibly by not later than Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Aerial images. We hinted at this topic yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you update the Trial Chamber on any pending issues that remain between you on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The trickiest issue is about the United States and what was needed. All that was worked out a long time ago. I believe Mr. Ostojic just wants to make his arguments about why they should not be admissible, and I think that's just where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We've objected to the aerial images at the outset, and I think that if you examine Mr. Butler's testimony when questioning him about those aerial images, he concedes that no one was able to either change or alter, or whichever word we wish to use, manipulate those documents. We saw early on the case 18 months that Mr. Ruez acknowledged that indeed they were inconsistent, some of the aerial images, and I know the Court raised the issue that we should use the word "different" as opposed to "inconsistent" during that testimony. There are differences and then on its face and the Court can observe, there are differences in the testimony from Mr. Butler who says that they were unable to make any alterations, and compared to what Mr. Ruez said that in fact he was able to remove certain dates and perhaps even certain times from those aerial images. We also have tried to show the Court, and I have to say this although the Court restricted me today because it's an argument, that what we and the Court can take at judicial notice is that aerial images were used with the United Nations and the Security Council in 1998 to establish that there were purportedly weapons of mass destruction, unrelated to this case. Ultimately, it has been found that those aerial images were either misrepresented to the United Nations, the Security Council, and the public, that they did not find the weapons of mass destruction that were paraded around by the same United States that is telling us, supposedly, that what is depicted on those aerial images should be accepted as a fact. When you compare that and if you accept it as judicial notice that those aerial images can mean one thing to one party and do not necessarily mean that which a party submits that it shows, I think that they have not established the proper foundation or authenticity for the documents to be admitted into evidence. It's our submission that the documents should be rejected at whole, given alone Mr. Butler's affirmation that no one was able to remove or strike out any portions of those aerial images, which is in direct contravention to what Mr. Ruez said when he acknowledged he removed the date. And if we remember, there was a specific box underneath the verbiage on the top of the aerial image with just a blank box, and then if we compare that with the specific emblem that's on one, I think, 236, of one of the aerial images, which shows that they could have removed it from time to time. For those reasons we submit that the aerial images should not be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, but do you wish to comment on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to --
